main.title: Macintosh 128K
main.summary: The Macintosh, later rebranded as the Macintosh 128K, is the original Macintosh personal computer from Apple.

cards.heading: Macintosh 128K
cards.text:
The Macintosh, later rebranded as the Macintosh 128K, is the original Macintosh personal computer from Apple. It is the first successful mass-market all-in-one desktop personal computer with a graphical user interface, built-in screen and mouse. It was pivotal in establishing desktop publishing as a general office function. A motherboard, a 9 in (23 cm) monochrome CRT monitor, and a floppy drive are all integrated into a beige case with an integrated carrying handle. As for peripherals, it has a keyboard and single-button mouse.

The Macintosh was introduced by a television commercial titled "1984" during Super Bowl XVIII on January 22, 1984, directed by Ridley Scott. Sales were strong at its initial release on January 24, 1984, at US$2,495 (equivalent to $7,700 in 2025), and reached 70,000 units on May 3, 1984. Upon the release of its successor, the Macintosh 512K, it was rebranded as the Macintosh 128K.

main.title: Neuromancer
main.summary: Neuromancer is a 1984 science fiction novel by William Gibson.

cards.heading: Neuromancer
cards.text:
Neuromancer is a 1984 science fiction novel by William Gibson. Set in the near future, the narrative follows Case, a computer hacker enlisted into a crew by a powerful artificial intelligence and a traumatised former soldier to complete a high-stakes heist. It was Gibson's debut novel and, after its success, served as the first entry in the Sprawl trilogy, followed by Count Zero (1986) and Mona Lisa Overdrive (1988).

Gibson had primarily written countercultural short stories for science-fiction periodicals before Neuromancer. Influences on the novel include the detective stories of Raymond Chandler, the comic art of Jean Giraud, and William S. Burroughs's Naked Lunch (1959). Neuromancer expanded and popularised the setting and concepts of an earlier Gibson story, "Burning Chrome" (1981), which introduced cyberspace—a digital space traversable by humans—and "jacking in", a bio-mechanical method of interfacing with computers.

main.title: The NeverEnding Story
main.subtitle: A reader becomes part of the world inside his book
main.summary: Wolfgang Petersen's The NeverEnding Story brings Michael Ende's fantasy novel to the screen through two boys: Bastian, who discovers an unusual book, and Atreyu, the young hero inside it. Released in West Germany on 6 April 1984, the film follows a reader whose involvement gradually becomes essential to the story he is reading.

cards.heading: A book opens another world
cards.text: Wolfgang Petersen's The NeverEnding Story brings Michael Ende's fantasy novel to the screen through two boys: Bastian, who discovers an unusual book, and Atreyu, the young hero inside it. Released in West Germany on 6 April 1984, the film follows a reader whose involvement gradually becomes essential to the story he is reading.

cards.heading: The boy in the attic
cards.text: Bastian retreats from school into an attic, where the book introduces Fantasia, a land being consumed by the Nothing. Atreyu must find a way to save its ailing Childlike Empress. His journey passes through swamps, monumental gates and encounters with creatures such as Falkor, the luckdragon. The film repeatedly returns to Bastian reacting to these events. Reading gives the adventure a second setting, and the distance between the quiet attic and the threatened world begins to shrink.

cards.heading: Giving fantasy a physical form
cards.text: Its creatures have a physical presence: fur, scales, stone and moving faces make Fantasia feel inhabited. Falkor offers a particularly warm contrast to the vast spaces and dangers of Atreyu's journey. The music also gave the film two familiar identities. Klaus Doldinger composed its German score; Giorgio Moroder contributed music to the international version, including the title song sung by Limahl. The film's images and that soaring pop refrain became closely associated with one another.

main.title: Atari ST
main.summary: Atari ST is a line of personal computers from Atari Corporation and the successor to the company's 8-bit computers.

cards.heading: Atari ST
cards.text:
Atari ST is a line of personal computers from Atari Corporation and the successor to the company's 8-bit computers. The initial model, the Atari 520ST, had limited release in April–June 1985, and was widely available in July. It was the first personal computer with a bitmapped color graphical user interface, using a version of Digital Research's GEM environment from February 1985. The Atari 1040ST, released in 1986 with 1 MB of memory, was the first home computer with a cost per kilobyte of RAM under US$1/KB.

After Jack Tramiel purchased the assets of the Atari, Inc. consumer division in 1984 to create Atari Corporation, the 520ST was designed in five months by a small team led by Shiraz Shivji. Alongside the Macintosh, Amiga, Apple IIGS, and Archimedes, the ST is part of a mid-1980s generation of computers with 16 or 32-bit processors, 256 KB or more of RAM, and mouse-controlled graphical user interfaces. "ST" officially stands for "Sixteen/Thirty-two", referring to the Motorola 68000's 16-bit external bus and 32-bit internals.

main.title: Back to the Future
main.summary: Back to the Future sent teenager Marty McFly from 1985 to 1955 in a DeLorean time machine.

cards.heading: Back to the Future
cards.text: Back to the Future sent teenager Marty McFly from 1985 to 1955 in a DeLorean time machine. His arrival disrupts his parents' first meeting, placing his own future at risk. Marty must bring them together while finding a way home with scientist Emmett Brown. Robert Zemeckis directed the film from a screenplay written with Bob Gale. They had developed the idea in 1980, but studios rejected it repeatedly before Universal backed the project. Michael J. Fox ultimately played Marty, pairing the family comedy with the practical problems created by travelling into the past.

main.title: Live Aid
main.summary: Live Aid was a two-venue benefit concert and music-based fund-raising initiative held on Saturday, 13 July 1985.

cards.heading: Live Aid
cards.text:
Live Aid was a two-venue benefit concert and music-based fund-raising initiative held on Saturday, 13 July 1985. The event was organised by Bob Geldof and Midge Ure to raise further funds for relief of the 1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia, a movement that started with the release of the successful charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" in December 1984. Billed as the "global jukebox", Live Aid was held simultaneously at Wembley Stadium in London and John F. Kennedy Stadium in Philadelphia.

On the same day, concerts inspired by the initiative were held in other countries, such as the Soviet Union, Canada, Japan, Yugoslavia, Austria, Australia, and West Germany. It was one of the largest satellite link-ups and television broadcasts of all time. An estimated audience of 1.9 billion people in 150 nations watched the live broadcast, nearly 40 percent of the world population.

main.title: Studio Ghibli
main.summary: Hayao Miyazaki, Isao Takahata and Toshio Suzuki founded Studio Ghibli on June 15, 1985, establishing the Japanese animation studio behind My Neighbor Totoro and Spirited Away.

cards.heading: Studio Ghibli
cards.text: Studio Ghibli Inc. is a Japanese animation studio based in Koganei, Tokyo. It was founded on June 15, 1985, by directors Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata and producer Toshio Suzuki, after acquiring Topcraft's assets. It has a strong presence in the animation industry and has expanded its portfolio to include various media such as short subjects, television commercials and two television films. The studio's work is highly acclaimed by both critics and audiences and has been recognized with numerous awards. Their mascot and most recognizable character is Totoro from the 1988 film My Neighbor Totoro, a giant spirit inspired by raccoon dogs (tanuki) and cats (neko). Among the studio's highest-grossing films are Princess Mononoke (1997), Spirited Away (2001), Howl's Moving Castle (2004), Ponyo (2008), and The Boy and the Heron (2023).

main.title: We Are the World
main.summary: "We Are the World" is a charity single recorded by the supergroup USA for Africa in 1985.

cards.heading: We Are the World
cards.text:
"We Are the World" is a charity single recorded by the supergroup USA for Africa in 1985. It was written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie and produced by Quincy Jones for the album We Are the World to raise money for the 1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia. With sales in excess of 20 million physical copies, it is the eighth-best-selling single of all time.

After the British group Band Aid released the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" in 1984, the musician and activist Harry Belafonte decided to create an American single for African famine relief. The agent Ken Kragen enlisted several musicians for the project. Jackson and Richie completed the writing the night before the first recording session on January 28, 1985. The recording brought together some of the era's best-known recording artists, including Bruce Springsteen, Cyndi Lauper, Paul Simon, Stevie Wonder, and Tina Turner.

main.title: Amiga 1000
main.summary: The Amiga 1000, also known as the A1000, is the first personal computer released by Commodore International in the Amiga line.

cards.heading: Amiga 1000
cards.text: The Amiga 1000, also known as the A1000, is the first personal computer released by Commodore International in the Amiga line. It combines the 16/32-bit Motorola 68000 CPU which was powerful by 1985 standards with one of the most advanced graphics and sound systems in its class. It runs a preemptive multitasking operating system that fits into 256 KB of read-only memory and was shipped with 256 KB of RAM. The primary memory can be expanded internally with a manufacturer-supplied 256 KB module for a total of 512 KB of RAM. Using the external slot the primary memory can be expanded up to 8.5 MB.

main.title: Chernobyl disaster
main.summary: Reactor 4 at the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded on 26 April 1986 near Pripyat in Soviet Ukraine.

cards.heading: Chernobyl disaster
cards.text: Reactor 4 at the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded on 26 April 1986 near Pripyat in Soviet Ukraine. Operators were testing how cooling systems would function during a blackout after an accidental fall in reactor power. Under those conditions, design flaws caused a power surge during shutdown. The explosion released large quantities of radioactive material, killed dozens directly and led to a lasting exclusion zone. More than 500,000 people took part in the response. The disaster received the highest rating on the International Nuclear Event Scale and left extensive environmental and health consequences.
